Neurology · published research

Parkinson's disease (PD)

Randomized studies report no consistent improvement across Parkinson’s motor outcomes: one feasibility trial found no between-group difference, and a later 63-person trial also found no active-versus-sham difference after its randomized phases. Some smaller reports show changes in selected gait or posture measures.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Randomized studies report no consistent improvement across Parkinson’s motor outcomes: one feasibility trial found no between-group difference, and a later 63-person trial also found no active-versus-sham difference after its randomized phases. Some smaller reports show changes in selected gait or posture measures.

Summary of the Evidence

The Parkinson's disease category contains 68 unique titles: 16 human research reports, 31 animal publications, eight in-vitro publications and 15 secondary or protocol records. Human reports include five randomized publications, seven other clinical reports and four case series. Secondary records include ten reviews, two systematic reviews, one protocol and two editorials or commentaries. One paper combines a human cohort with in-vitro work, and reviews overlap with primary publications. Animal species tags also overlap where a paper used more than one model. Longitudinal follow-up publications should not be treated as new cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

Herkes et al. conducted a small parallel randomized feasibility study and found no significant difference between groups at any assessment point (Herkes et al. 2023). A post-hoc analysis of a related randomized helmet study found no group difference in total MDS-UPDRS-III score, although some facial and limb sub-scores changed (McGee et al. 2023). In a 63-person randomized trial, active treatment did not differ significantly from sham after the randomized phases; a later 48-week comparison of participants who continued treatment with those who did not was non-randomized and cannot establish a causal long-term effect (Saltmarche et al. 2025). Another randomized study found PBM-related changes in selected posturography outcomes but no additive effect with exercise across the measured outcomes (Santos et al. 2025). Liebert et al.'s 2024 five-year follow-up reports on the small participant group first described in 2021, not a new independent cohort (PubMed).

Animal evidence

Thirty-one animal publications include toxin-induced and genetic models, with mouse, rat, monkey and fruit-fly studies. Many report motor or neuronal changes after PBM, but the models and treatment routes differ and animal outcomes do not show slowed human progression.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Eight publications use in-vitro cell models, including human-derived neuronal or cybrid cells. They investigate mitochondrial function or cellular stress.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Studies apply light transcranially, intranasally or to other body regions. Wavelengths include red visible light near 635–670 nm and near-infrared light around 810–940 nm. Devices include lasers and LEDs, and schedules range from single exposures to long-term home treatment. These route and dose differences matter, particularly because light delivered to the scalp is not equivalent to a device applied inside the nose or to another body site.

Interpretation

The literature supports feasibility and possible changes in selected motor measures, but randomized evidence does not show a consistent clinical effect or disease-modifying benefit. Mixed endpoints, small cohorts and overlapping long-term reports leave the size and durability of any benefit uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term motor or balance outcomes because randomized studies are small and results differ by measure. Very low for slowing disease progression or producing sustained daily-function gains.
Publications and records68 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Five randomized publication reports and several uncontrolled reports describe mixed motor results, with some follow-up articles reusing earlier participant cohorts. The largest recent sham-controlled trial found no active-versus-sham difference after the randomized phases. Longer controlled studies should use prespecified motor and non-motor outcomes and separate randomized results from open follow-up.
